crossrefs.note: The 'blind leading the blind' verse appears almost word for word in both Upanishads.
'This Self is not attained by discourse, nor by intellect, nor by much learning.'
'There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars.'
'It is not born, nor does it die.' The Gītā reuses the Kaṭha's verse almost entirely.
'If the slayer thinks he slays…' Both close with the same line: it neither slays nor is slain.
Both speak of the Self as a 'wonder': wondrous the one who teaches it, wondrous the one who sees it.
The goal 'that all the Vedas declare' (Kaṭha) and 'that the knowers of the Veda call imperishable' (Gītā).
The same image, in different words: the eternal aśvattha tree with its roots above and branches below.
The two birds on one tree come from the Ṛgveda's riddle hymn of Dīrghatamas.
The two birds on one tree, in both the Śvetāśvatara and the Muṇḍaka.
The bird that grieves until it sees the other, the Lord.
‘There the sun does not shine, nor moon nor stars.’
‘Smaller than the small, greater than the great.’
The golden lid over the face of truth: the Īśā's closing verses also close the Bṛhadāraṇyaka's fifth chapter.
‘With hands and feet everywhere’: the Gītā takes up the Śvetāśvatara's verse.
‘Sun-coloured, beyond the darkness’: the same image of the Person in the Gītā.
The senses, the mind, the intellect and beyond: the Kaṭha's ladder in the Gītā.
